voiceover: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculator that was never finished.
visual: Museum photo of Babbage’s engine parts, open-access

voiceover: Ada Lovelace translated an article about it and added notes longer than the article itself.
visual: Re-creation: two paper stacks, hers taller

voiceover: One note set out steps for the machine to calculate a sequence of numbers.
visual: Simple graphic: table of steps

voiceover: She also guessed machines could do more than math. Who should I cover next?
visual: Portrait, slow zoom

voiceover: European courts once put pigs on trial. Really.
visual: Medieval manuscript image of a courtroom (public domain)

voiceover: From roughly the 1300s to the 1700s, records describe animals charged in courts across Europe.
visual: Map of Europe with case pins

voiceover: Pigs were common defendants, usually for causing harm on farms. Some cases had a formal hearing and a verdict.
visual: Re-creation: pig silhouette in a dock

voiceover: Church courts handled pests too. Rats and insects that ate crops were sometimes formally warned to leave.
visual: Manuscript margin drawing of insects (public domain)

voiceover: Historians link these trials to ideas about order and justice: even harm by an animal needed a public answer.
visual: Simple graphic: scales of justice

voiceover: A collection of cases was published in 1906. Which animal would you put on trial today?
visual: Courtroom image, slow zoom

voiceover: The first powered flight lasted only twelve seconds.
visual: Public-domain photo of the 1903 Wright Flyer

voiceover: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright tested their engine-powered Flyer near Kitty Hawk.
visual: Map pin on Kitty Hawk, North Carolina

voiceover: Orville flew first. The plane covered about 120 feet, less than the wingspan of a large jet.
visual: Diagram: 120 feet vs jet wingspan

voiceover: They flew four times that day. The longest flight, by Wilbur, lasted about 59 seconds.
visual: Timeline graphic: four flights, durations

voiceover: A gust of wind then damaged the plane, and it never flew again. It is now in a museum.
visual: Museum photo of the Flyer, open-access

voiceover: Sixty-six years later, people walked on the Moon. What invention do you think moved fastest?
visual: Timeline: 1903 → 1969

voiceover: Ice from frozen ponds once sailed to the tropics.
visual: Period engraving of ice harvesting (public domain)

voiceover: In 1806, a Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor shipped ice to the Caribbean. People laughed at him.
visual: Map: Boston to the Caribbean

voiceover: Workers sawed blocks from frozen ponds in winter and packed them in sawdust to slow the melting.
visual: Re-creation: ice blocks stacked in sawdust

voiceover: Tudor built insulated ice houses at the ports. Over the years his ice trade became profitable.
visual: Simple diagram: ice house walls

voiceover: By the 1830s, ships even carried New England ice to India, a voyage of several months.
visual: Map: route around Africa to India

voiceover: Ice was once a luxury import. Which everyday item do you think was once a luxury?
visual: Engraving, slow zoom

voiceover: Six centuries old, and nobody can read this book.
visual: Public-domain scan of a Voynich manuscript page

voiceover: It is called the Voynich manuscript, after a book dealer who bought it in 1912.
visual: Label graphic: MS 408, Yale

voiceover: Its vellum pages were radiocarbon dated to the early 1400s. They hold about 240 pages of unknown script.
visual: Timeline graphic: early 1400s marker

voiceover: There are drawings of plants nobody has identified, star charts and bathing figures. Some pages fold out.
visual: Slow pan over drawings (public domain scans)

voiceover: Professional code-breakers and many researchers have tried. No proposed reading has been widely accepted.
visual: Re-creation: notes and crossed-out guesses

voiceover: It sits at Yale today. Is it a code, a lost language, or a hoax?
visual: Page scan, slow zoom

voiceover: The pyramids weren’t built by slaves. Here’s the evidence.
visual: Photo of the Giza pyramids, open-licence

voiceover: The popular version shows whipped slaves dragging stones. It spread through old histories and films.
visual: Re-creation: red question mark over the scene

voiceover: Archaeologists found a workers’ town near Giza, with bakeries, sleeping halls and many animal bones from food.
visual: Map: workers’ town beside the pyramids

voiceover: They also found workers’ tombs close to the pyramids. Enslaved people would not usually get such burials.
visual: Photo of tomb remains, open-licence

voiceover: The likely picture is skilled crews plus rotating labourers called up for a season, paid partly in food.
visual: Simple graphic: crew rotation diagram

voiceover: Hard work, but not slavery as shown in films. What ancient myth should I check next?
visual: Pyramids at sunset, slow zoom

voiceover: Medieval people didn’t all die at thirty. Averages mislead.
visual: Medieval painting of elderly villagers (public domain)

voiceover: You may have heard that medieval life expectancy was around 30, so adults died young.
visual: Re-creation: number 30 with red question mark

voiceover: But an average includes babies and children. Many children died very young, which pulls the average far down.
visual: Simple chart: ages spread, average line drops

voiceover: If you survived childhood, your chances changed. Many adults lived into their fifties or sixties, some much longer.
visual: Chart: adult ages shift right

voiceover: So 30 was the average at birth, not a typical age of death for grown adults.
visual: Timeline graphic: birth → adulthood

voiceover: One number, two meanings. What history statistic confused you as a kid?
visual: Painting, slow zoom

voiceover: Decades before Columbus, Chinese fleets reached East Africa.
visual: Old map of the Indian Ocean (public domain)

voiceover: Between 1405 and 1433, the admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages for the Ming emperors.
visual: Timeline graphic: seven voyage markers

voiceover: The fleets were huge. The first reportedly carried around 27,000 people on many ships.
visual: Simple graphic: fleet of ship icons

voiceover: They sailed to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the coast of East Africa, trading and showing Ming power.
visual: Map: routes across the Indian Ocean

voiceover: The exact size of the biggest ships is debated. Some accounts may exaggerate them.
visual: Re-creation: ship outline with question mark

voiceover: After 1433 the voyages stopped, and the fleets were never sent again. Why do you think China ended them?
visual: Map, slow zoom out

voiceover: In 1844, a message crossed forty miles almost instantly.
visual: Public-domain photo of a Morse telegraph key

voiceover: Before that, news traveled as fast as a horse, a train or a ship could carry it.
visual: Re-creation: horse, train and ship icons

voiceover: Samuel Morse and his partners built a telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore, about 40 miles.
visual: Map: line between the two cities

voiceover: On May 24, 1844, Morse tapped out a Bible phrase: what hath God wrought. It arrived in Baltimore.
visual: Paper tape graphic with dots and dashes

voiceover: Within a few decades, telegraph wires crossed continents and, from 1866, the Atlantic Ocean.
visual: Map: wires spread across continents

voiceover: Words at the speed of electricity. What would your first message be?
visual: Telegraph key, slow zoom

voiceover: Britain once taxed people for their windows.
visual: Photo of a bricked-up window, own photo or open-licence

voiceover: In 1696, England introduced a window tax. Houses with more windows paid more.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1696 marker

voiceover: The idea was simple. Windows could be counted from the street, so officials didn’t need to go inside.
visual: Re-creation: official counting windows

voiceover: Many owners bricked up windows to pay less. You can still see blocked windows on some old buildings.
visual: Photo series of blocked windows

voiceover: Critics said it cut light and fresh air in crowded homes. The tax was finally abolished in 1851.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1696 → 1851

voiceover: It lasted 155 years. Have you ever spotted a bricked-up window near you?
visual: Slow zoom on the blocked window

voiceover: In 1752, Britain skipped eleven days in one night.
visual: Re-creation: calendar page, Sept 3–13 crossed out

voiceover: The old Julian calendar ran a little long, so it slowly drifted away from the seasons.
visual: Diagram: calendar vs sun drift

voiceover: Catholic countries had switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1582. Britain waited about 170 years.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1582 → 1752

voiceover: To catch up, Wednesday, September 2, 1752 was followed by Thursday, September 14. The days between never happened.
visual: Calendar graphic: 2 jumps to 14

voiceover: There’s a famous story about riots demanding the lost days back. Evidence for real riots is thin.
visual: Re-creation: crowd with red question mark

voiceover: The same change reached the American colonies. Which day would you happily skip?
visual: Calendar page, slow zoom

voiceover: Kitchens once used small dogs to turn the roast.
visual: Period illustration of a turnspit wheel (public domain)

voiceover: Meat was roasted on a spit in front of the fire, and it had to keep turning.
visual: Re-creation: spit in front of a fireplace

voiceover: In many British kitchens, a small breed called the turnspit dog ran inside a wooden wheel on the wall.
visual: Diagram: wheel linked to spit by a belt

voiceover: The wheel was linked to the spit, so as the dog ran, the meat turned. Shifts could be long.
visual: Simple animation: wheel turns, spit turns

voiceover: Mechanical spits replaced them in the 1800s, and the breed died out. A preserved one is in a Welsh museum.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1500s → 1800s

voiceover: A whole breed gone with one job. Which old job should I explain next?
visual: Illustration, slow zoom

voiceover: Amelia Earhart vanished in 1937. Nobody found her plane.
visual: Public-domain photo of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra

voiceover: Earhart was famous already. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
visual: Map: Atlantic route

voiceover: In 1937, she and navigator Fred Noonan set out to fly around the world near the equator.
visual: Map: round-the-world route

voiceover: On July 2, they left New Guinea for Howland Island, a tiny speck in the Pacific. They never arrived.
visual: Map: route ends before Howland Island

voiceover: A huge search found nothing. Theories include running out of fuel at sea or landing on another island.
visual: Re-creation: search ships on a map

voiceover: None has been proven. What do you think happened on that last flight?
visual: Slow zoom on the empty ocean

voiceover: This Roman dome has stood for nearly 1,900 years.
visual: Public-domain photo of the Pantheon dome interior

voiceover: The Pantheon in Rome was rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian around AD 125, and it is still in use.
visual: Map pin on Rome

voiceover: Its dome is about 43 metres across. It has no steel inside: it is unreinforced concrete.
visual: Diagram: dome cross-section with measurement

voiceover: The builders made the concrete lighter toward the top, using lighter stone mixed in, and thinner walls.
visual: Diagram: heavy at base, light at top

voiceover: At the very top is an open hole, the oculus, about nine metres wide. Rain falls straight in.
visual: Photo looking up at the oculus

voiceover: Still the largest dome of its kind. Which ancient building would you visit first?
visual: Slow zoom on the oculus

voiceover: One workshop in Mainz changed how Europe made books.
visual: Public-domain scan of a Gutenberg Bible page

voiceover: Before the 1450s, almost every book in Europe was copied by hand, often taking months.
visual: Manuscript illustration of a scribe (public domain)

voiceover: Johannes Gutenberg developed a system of movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine presses.
visual: Diagram: type pieces, ink, press

voiceover: Around 1455 his workshop finished a large Latin Bible. Historians estimate about 180 copies were printed.
visual: Timeline graphic: c. 1455 marker

voiceover: Gutenberg lost his workshop to his financial partner after a lawsuit. Printing spread across Europe anyway.
visual: Map: printing spreads city by city

voiceover: Fewer than 50 copies survive today. Which book would you have printed first?
visual: Page scan, slow zoom

voiceover: On long voyages, sailors feared scurvy more than storms.
visual: Period painting of a sailing warship (public domain)

voiceover: Scurvy caused weakness and bleeding gums on long voyages. We now know it comes from lacking vitamin C.
visual: Re-creation: ship’s biscuit and salt meat

voiceover: In 1747, ship’s surgeon James Lind tested treatments on twelve sick sailors, in pairs.
visual: Diagram: six pairs, six treatments

voiceover: The pair given oranges and lemons improved fastest. It was one of the earliest controlled trials in medicine.
visual: Diagram: citrus pair highlighted

voiceover: But the Navy didn’t act at once. Lemon juice became a routine ration only around 1795.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1747 → 1795

voiceover: Nearly fifty years for a fix. Which good idea do you think took too long?
visual: Lemon crate, slow zoom

voiceover: In 1895, a glowing screen led to the X-ray.
visual: Public-domain X-ray image of a hand with a ring

voiceover: On November 8, Wilhelm Röntgen was testing a covered electric tube in his German lab.
visual: Re-creation: lab bench with a glass tube

voiceover: A coated screen across the room started to glow, even though the tube was covered.
visual: Diagram: invisible rays reach a screen

voiceover: He called the unknown rays X-rays. Weeks later he made an image of his wife’s hand, showing bones and a ring.
visual: Slow zoom on the hand image

voiceover: Doctors began using X-rays within months. In 1901 Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1895 → 1901

voiceover: An accident changed medicine. Which accidental discovery surprises you most?
visual: Hand X-ray, slow zoom out

voiceover: English kings banned football again and again.
visual: Medieval manuscript drawing of a ball game (public domain)

voiceover: Medieval football wasn’t a tidy match. Crowds chased a ball through streets, with few rules.
visual: Re-creation: crowd silhouettes and a ball

voiceover: In 1314, a proclamation in London banned it, worried about noise and disorder in the city.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1314 marker

voiceover: Later, Edward III wanted men practising archery for war instead of playing ball games.
visual: Manuscript drawing of archers (public domain)

voiceover: Similar bans were repeated for centuries, in England and in Scotland, which suggests people kept playing anyway.
visual: Timeline graphic: repeated ban markers

voiceover: Football outlasted every single ban, and today it fills stadiums. Which modern sport would annoy a medieval king most?
visual: Ball game drawing, slow zoom

voiceover: One golden spike finished a railroad across America.
visual: Public-domain photo of the 1869 ceremony

voiceover: Two companies built toward each other, one from California and one from the Midwest.
visual: Map: two lines approaching each other

voiceover: Thousands of workers, many from China and Ireland, laid the track across mountains and plains.
visual: Period photo of track workers (public domain)

voiceover: On May 10, 1869, the lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah. A telegraph sent one word: done.
visual: Map pin on Promontory Summit

voiceover: The golden spike was removed right after the ceremony. It is kept at a Stanford museum today.
visual: Museum photo of the spike, open-access

voiceover: A trip of weeks or months became about a week. Which turning-point day should I cover next?
visual: Map, slow zoom out

voiceover: Ancient Romans had street food counters, like fast food.
visual: Public-domain photo of a Pompeii food counter

voiceover: In Pompeii, archaeologists have found many counters called thermopolia along the streets.
visual: Map of Pompeii with counter pins

voiceover: Each had a masonry counter with large jars set into the top, for hot or dry food.
visual: Diagram: counter with jars

voiceover: Many city flats had no proper kitchen, so buying food outside was part of everyday life.
visual: Re-creation: small flat without a kitchen

voiceover: Some counters were painted with animals and scenes. Remains in jars suggest dishes with meat, fish and beans.
visual: Close-up of a painted counter, open-licence

voiceover: Lunch on the go, about 2,000 years ago. What would you order in Pompeii?
visual: Counter, slow zoom

voiceover: In 1872, a ship was found drifting, nobody aboard.
visual: Public-domain painting of the Mary Celeste

voiceover: The Mary Celeste had left New York for Genoa, carrying barrels of industrial alcohol.
visual: Map: New York to Genoa route

voiceover: A month later, another ship found her drifting near the Azores. The crew of ten was gone.
visual: Map pin near the Azores

voiceover: Her cargo was mostly intact and there was food on board. Her lifeboat was missing.
visual: Re-creation: empty davits where a boat hung

voiceover: One common theory: fear of a leak or fumes made them leave in the lifeboat, then they were lost.
visual: Diagram: ship and small boat drifting apart

voiceover: Nobody was ever found. What do you think made them leave the ship?
visual: Painting, slow zoom

voiceover: This broken stone let people read hieroglyphs again.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Rosetta Stone

voiceover: For over a thousand years, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. The knowledge had been lost.
visual: Public-domain photo of temple hieroglyphs

voiceover: In 1799, French soldiers in Egypt found a carved slab near the town of Rosetta.
visual: Map pin on Rosetta, Nile Delta

voiceover: It carried one decree from 196 BC, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script and in ancient Greek.
visual: Diagram: three bands of text

voiceover: Scholars could read the Greek. So they had the same message in a script they knew, beside two they didn’t.
visual: Diagram: Greek band lit, arrows to others

voiceover: Names like Ptolemy sat inside oval frames called cartouches. Matching those names gave the first sound values.
visual: Close-up of a cartouche (public domain)

voiceover: In 1822, Jean-François Champollion announced he could read the system. Egypt’s own words could be read again.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1799 → 1822

voiceover: The stone is in the British Museum. Which lost script would you want to read?
visual: Slow zoom on the stone

voiceover: Vikings never wore horned helmets into battle.
visual: 1800s painting of a horned warrior (public domain), red X

voiceover: That image is everywhere: cartoons, sports logos, costumes. But archaeologists have never found a Viking-age helmet with horns.
visual: Your own quick doodles of horned helmets

voiceover: The best-preserved one, the Gjermundbu helmet, was found in Norway in 1943. It’s a rounded iron cap with eye guards.
visual: Line drawing of the Gjermundbu helmet

voiceover: No horns. Horns would be a terrible idea in a fight: they give a blade something to catch.
visual: Re-creation: helmet outline, horns fade out

voiceover: So where did the horns come from? Mostly the 1800s. Painters and costume designers gave Norse heroes horns and wings to look dramatic.
visual: Timeline graphic: 800 → 1800s

voiceover: A famous example: the first full staging of Wagner’s Ring cycle in 1876, whose costumes gave several characters horned helmets.
visual: Period stage-design sketch (public domain)

voiceover: Real horned helmets do exist, found in Denmark. But they’re Bronze Age ceremonial pieces, well over a thousand years older than the Viking age.
visual: Map of Denmark, pin drops; timeline zooms out

voiceover: What history fact did you learn as a kid that turned out wrong?
visual: Freeze on the X-stamped painting

voiceover: They crossed thousands of miles of ocean without maps.
visual: Map of the Pacific triangle: Hawaii, New Zealand, Rapa Nui

voiceover: Over many centuries, Polynesian navigators settled islands spread across a huge triangle of the Pacific.
visual: Map: arrows spread island to island

voiceover: The last big ones, like Hawaii and New Zealand, were settled roughly 800 to 1,000 years ago.
visual: Timeline graphic: settlement dates, rounded

voiceover: Navigators read the night sky. They memorized where stars rose and set on the horizon, and steered by them.
visual: Re-creation: star compass circle

voiceover: By day they felt ocean swells against the hull. Swell patterns bend around islands long before land appears.
visual: Diagram: swells bending around an island

voiceover: Birds helped too. Some seabirds fly out to fish in the morning and return to land at dusk.
visual: Simple graphic: bird flight lines toward an island

voiceover: Some once argued these islands were found by accident. Planned voyages explain the evidence better.
visual: Map: two-way voyage arrows

voiceover: Stars, waves and birds. Which clue would you trust most on open water?
visual: Starry sky over ocean, slow zoom

voiceover: Galileo didn’t invent the telescope. Here’s who did.
visual: Public-domain drawing of an early telescope

voiceover: In 1608, Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey sought a patent for a device making distant things look closer.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1608 marker

voiceover: He wasn’t the only one. Other Dutch makers claimed it too, so the patent was not granted.
visual: Re-creation: three claim papers

voiceover: News spread fast. In 1609, Galileo Galilei in Italy heard about it and built his own, much stronger version.
visual: Map: Netherlands to Italy arrow

voiceover: Then he did what made him famous: he pointed it at the sky and wrote down what he saw.
visual: Museum photo of Galileo’s telescope, open-access

voiceover: He saw mountains on the Moon and, in 1610, four moons circling Jupiter.
visual: Simple graphic: Jupiter with four dots

voiceover: So he didn’t invent it. He turned a curiosity into a tool for astronomy.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1608 → 1610

voiceover: Which inventor do you think gets credit for someone else’s idea?
visual: Telescope drawing, slow zoom

voiceover: Early British vehicles needed a walker carrying a flag.
visual: Re-creation: walker with red flag ahead of a steam vehicle

voiceover: In 1865, Britain passed a Locomotive Act for steam-powered vehicles on public roads.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1865 marker

voiceover: The speed limit was four miles an hour in the country and two miles an hour in towns.
visual: Simple graphic: speedometer at 4 and 2

voiceover: Each vehicle needed a crew, and one person had to walk in front, warning riders and horses, carrying a red flag.
visual: Diagram: crew positions around the vehicle

voiceover: Lawmakers worried about frightened horses, damaged roads and noisy machines. Horses were still the main traffic.
visual: Period engraving of a busy road (public domain)

voiceover: In 1878 the flag rule was relaxed. Early petrol cars arrived, still under strict rules.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1865 → 1878

voiceover: In 1896 a new law raised the limit to 14 miles an hour. Drivers celebrated with a run to Brighton.
visual: Map: London to Brighton route

voiceover: Which rule of today will look strange in 100 years?
visual: Flag walker, slow zoom

voiceover: London smelled so bad in 1858, it built sewers.
visual: Period cartoon of the Thames (public domain)

voiceover: For years, London’s sewage and waste flowed straight into the River Thames, the same river many drew water from.
visual: Map of the Thames through London

voiceover: In the hot summer of 1858, the river’s smell became so strong people called it the Great Stink.
visual: Timeline graphic: summer 1858

voiceover: Parliament sat right beside the river. Curtains were reportedly soaked in chemicals to block the smell.
visual: Engraving of the Houses of Parliament (public domain)

voiceover: Lawmakers who had delayed for years suddenly moved quickly and approved a huge sewer plan within weeks.
visual: Re-creation: papers stamped approved

voiceover: Engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed it: large brick tunnels that carried waste away from central London.
visual: Diagram: tunnels running beside the river

voiceover: The new system helped end the city’s cholera outbreaks, and parts of it are still in use today.
visual: Photo of a Victorian sewer tunnel, open-licence

voiceover: A bad smell changed a city. What hidden system in your town do you never think about?
visual: Thames map, slow zoom

voiceover: This tiny black stamp changed how letters got paid.
visual: Museum open-access image of the Penny Black

voiceover: Before 1840, British letters were usually paid for by the person receiving them, priced by distance and sheets.
visual: Re-creation: letter with postage marks

voiceover: That made post expensive and slow to collect. Some people refused letters to avoid paying.
visual: Simple graphic: letter returned to sender

voiceover: A reformer named Rowland Hill proposed one cheap rate, paid in advance by the sender.
visual: Timeline graphic: reform proposal

voiceover: In 1840, Britain introduced the uniform penny post. One penny sent a light letter anywhere in the country.
visual: Map of Britain, letters fly in all directions

voiceover: On May 6, 1840, the Penny Black became valid, the world’s first adhesive postage stamp.
visual: Close-up of the stamp

voiceover: Letter numbers rose sharply within a few years, and other countries soon introduced their own stamps.
visual: Map: stamps spread across countries

voiceover: Today, billions of stamps later, when did you last send a paper letter?
visual: Stamp, slow zoom

voiceover: Thousands of these seals survive. Nobody can read them.
visual: Museum open-access photo of an Indus seal

voiceover: The Indus civilization grew along rivers in today’s Pakistan and northwest India, about 4,500 years ago.
visual: Map of the Indus Valley region

voiceover: Its cities, like Mohenjo-daro, had planned streets, brick houses and covered drains.
visual: Public-domain photo of Mohenjo-daro ruins

voiceover: They also left thousands of small carved seals, often with an animal and a short row of symbols.
visual: Diagram: seal parts labelled

voiceover: The inscriptions are very short, usually just a few signs. That gives code-breakers little to work with.
visual: Simple graphic: five signs in a row

voiceover: There is no known bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, that pairs this script with a known one.
visual: Re-creation: Rosetta Stone outline, crossed out

voiceover: Many decipherments have been proposed. None is widely accepted, and scholars even debate what language it records.
visual: Re-creation: question marks over signs

voiceover: Which lost script do you think will be cracked next?
visual: Seal, slow zoom

voiceover: This corroded shipwreck lump is full of ancient gears.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Antikythera fragments

voiceover: In 1901, sponge divers recovered objects from an ancient wreck near the Greek island of Antikythera.
visual: Map pin on Antikythera

voiceover: Among statues and pottery were some lumps of corroded bronze. Months later someone noticed a gear wheel.
visual: Re-creation: museum crate with fragments

voiceover: Scans in modern times revealed dozens of interlocking gears and tiny inscriptions inside the fragments.
visual: Diagram: gear layout, simple outline

voiceover: It was likely made around the second or first century BC. Dates vary between studies.
visual: Timeline graphic: 200–1 BC range

voiceover: Turning a handle moved dials showing the Sun, the Moon and predicted eclipses.
visual: Diagram: front dial with pointers

voiceover: Nothing this complex is known again until the medieval astronomical clocks of Europe, many centuries later.
visual: Timeline graphic: gap to medieval clocks

voiceover: Who built it, and exactly why, is still unknown. Which ancient object would you want to study?
visual: Fragments, slow zoom

voiceover: Medieval chess pieces turned up on a Scottish island.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Lewis chessmen

voiceover: In 1831 a hoard of small carved figures was found on the Isle of Lewis, in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides.
visual: Map pin on the Isle of Lewis

voiceover: There were dozens of chess pieces: kings, queens, bishops, knights and warders, plus game pieces.
visual: Simple graphic: piece types in a row

voiceover: Most are carved from walrus ivory, some from whale teeth. They date to around the late 1100s.
visual: Close-up of the ivory carving, open-access

voiceover: Their style suggests they were probably made in Norway, perhaps in Trondheim, then carried west.
visual: Map: Norway to the Hebrides route

voiceover: How they ended up buried on Lewis is not known. A merchant’s stock is one idea.
visual: Re-creation: small bag buried in sand

voiceover: Some warders bite the tops of their shields, which makes them one of the most loved museum objects.
visual: Close-up of a shield-biting warder

voiceover: Which piece would you put on your board?
visual: Pieces lined up, slow zoom

voiceover: Ice crushed their ship. Every crew member survived.
visual: Public-domain photo of Endurance in pack ice

voiceover: In 1914, the explorer Ernest Shackleton sailed south, aiming to cross the whole of Antarctica on foot.
visual: Map of Antarctica with planned route

voiceover: In early 1915 his ship, Endurance, was trapped in sea ice. Months later the ice crushed it and it sank.
visual: Timeline graphic: trapped → sank

voiceover: The 28 men camped on drifting ice, then took three small boats to tiny Elephant Island.
visual: Map: drift and boat route

voiceover: Shackleton and five others sailed a small lifeboat about 800 miles to South Georgia to get help.
visual: Map: Elephant Island to South Georgia

voiceover: Then they crossed the island’s mountains to reach a whaling station. Rescue took several attempts.
visual: Simple graphic: mountain crossing line

voiceover: In August 1916, a Chilean ship rescued all the men left on Elephant Island.
visual: Public-domain photo of the rescue

voiceover: All of them came home. What quality would you most want in a leader?
visual: Endurance photo, slow zoom

voiceover: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
visual: Public-domain photo of Curie’s laboratory

voiceover: She was born in Warsaw in 1867 and moved to Paris to study physics and mathematics.
visual: Map: Warsaw to Paris

voiceover: With her husband Pierre, she studied the strange rays given off by uranium and other minerals.
visual: Re-creation: mineral sample and measuring device

voiceover: In 1898 they announced two new elements: polonium, named after Poland, and radium.
visual: Simple graphic: two element tiles

voiceover: In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. She was the first woman to win one.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1903 marker

voiceover: In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own, for her work on radium and polonium.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1903 → 1911

voiceover: Her notebooks are still radioactive today, and readers reportedly handle them with protective precautions.
visual: Re-creation: notebook in a lined box

voiceover: Her story is still taught worldwide. Which scientist do you think deserves more fame?
visual: Lab photo, slow zoom

voiceover: In 1795, Britain taxed people for powdering their hair.
visual: Period portrait with powdered wig (public domain)

voiceover: Powdered wigs and hair were high fashion in the 1700s. The powder was usually made from starch or flour.
visual: Re-creation: powder box and puff

voiceover: Britain was at war with France, and the government needed money. Food prices were also rising.
visual: Timeline graphic: 1795 marker

voiceover: When a peregrine falcon dives from high in the sky, it can top 300 kilometers per hour.

voiceover: It tucks its wings close to its body, turning itself into a streamlined dart.
visual: Simple diagram: wings tucked into a teardrop

voiceover: Bony structures in its nostrils are thought to help it breathe while air rushes past at that speed.
visual: Simple diagram: nostril with airflow arrows

visual: Stock clip: falcon on a city building ledge

voiceover: This jellyfish can turn its life clock backwards.
visual: Stock clip: tiny jellyfish pulsing in water

voiceover: Turritopsis dohrnii is smaller than your fingernail, and it has a rare trick.
visual: Scale graphic: jellyfish next to a fingernail

voiceover: When it’s stressed or damaged, the adult can turn back into a polyp, its early, rooted stage.
visual: Simple animation: jellyfish shrinking into a polyp

voiceover: That polyp then grows new jellyfish. In theory, the cycle can repeat again and again.
visual: Simple animation: polyp budding new jellyfish

voiceover: So people call it immortal. But it can still be eaten, or die from disease, like other animals.
visual: Simple graphic: fish icon near jellyfish

voiceover: These ants are farmers, not leaf eaters.
visual: Stock clip: leafcutter ants carrying leaf pieces

voiceover: Leafcutter ants slice pieces of leaves and carry them home, often many times their own weight.
visual: Close-up stock clip: ant cutting a leaf

voiceover: But they don’t eat the leaves. Inside the nest, smaller workers chew them into a soft pulp.
visual: Simple diagram: nest chamber cross-section

voiceover: The pulp feeds a fungus garden. The ants eat the fungus, feed it to their young, and weed out unwanted molds.
visual: Simple animation: leaves to fungus to ants

voiceover: Different worker sizes have different jobs, from cutting and carrying to guarding and gardening.
visual: Simple graphic: ants of four sizes, labeled jobs

voiceover: This bird can copy almost any sound it hears.
visual: Stock clip: superb lyrebird on forest floor

voiceover: The superb lyrebird lives in the damp forests of southeastern Australia, mostly foraging on the ground.
visual: Map of range: southeastern Australia

voiceover: Males sing long songs packed with copies of other birds, like kookaburras and whipbirds.
visual: Simple graphic: bird icons with music notes

voiceover: Some lyrebirds have been recorded copying human-made sounds too, such as camera shutters, car alarms and chainsaws.

voiceover: Sloths aren’t lazy. They’re running on low power.
visual: Stock clip: sloth hanging from a branch

voiceover: Sloths eat mostly leaves, which give very little energy and are hard to digest.
visual: Stock clip: sloth chewing leaves slowly

voiceover: One meal can take days or even weeks to work its way through their large, many-chambered stomachs.
visual: Simple diagram: stomach with chambers

voiceover: Moving slowly saves energy. Their muscles are small, and their body temperature runs lower than most mammals.
visual: Simple graphic: battery icon on low

voiceover: Slowness also helps them stay unnoticed. Algae can even grow in their fur, adding a greenish tint.
visual: Close-up stock clip of green-tinted fur

voiceover: Slow is a survival plan, not laziness. Which slow animal should I cover next?

voiceover: Some Komodo dragons have had babies without a father.
visual: Stock clip: Komodo dragon walking on sand

voiceover: The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard, up to about 3 meters long.
visual: Scale graphic: dragon next to a person outline

voiceover: It lives on a few Indonesian islands, including Komodo, the island it’s named after.
visual: Map of range: islands in Indonesia

voiceover: In zoos, female dragons kept without males have laid eggs that hatched. This is called parthenogenesis.
visual: Simple graphic: egg with a question mark

visual: Simple family-tree graphic: mother to sons

visual: Stock clip: horse dozing in a field

voiceover: That means a horse can doze on its feet without falling over, ready to move fast if startled.
visual: Stock clip: horse with head lowered, eyes half closed

voiceover: But for deep sleep, the kind with dreaming, a horse needs to lie down.
visual: Stock clip: horse lying in grass

voiceover: They often take that deep sleep in short spells, while other horses in the herd stay standing.
visual: Stock clip: herd with one horse lying down

voiceover: Passenger pigeons may have been the most numerous birds in North America, with billions alive at once.

voiceover: Their flocks were so large that people described them passing overhead for hours, even days, at a time.
visual: Simple animation: dense flock moving across the sky

visual: Timeline graphic: 1800s with falling line

visual: Stock clip: tiny hummingbird at a flower

voiceover: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
visual: Stock clip: octopus crawling over reef rocks

voiceover: Two of those hearts pump blood through the gills. The third pumps it to the rest of the body.
visual: Simple diagram: three hearts light up in turn

voiceover: And here’s the strange part: that third heart seems to stop beating while the octopus swims.
visual: Stock clip: octopus jetting, then crawling

voiceover: Why blue? Octopus blood carries oxygen with a copper-based protein called hemocyanin, not the iron-based one in ours.
visual: Split-screen graphic: copper vs iron

voiceover: Hemocyanin turns blue when it picks up oxygen, and it works well in cold water with little oxygen.
visual: Stock clip: dim, cold deep-water scene

voiceover: Then there’s the brain. Around two-thirds of an octopus’s nerve cells sit in its arms, not its head.
visual: Simple animation: dots spread into eight arms

voiceover: And those are arms, not tentacles. Octopuses have eight arms. Squid and cuttlefish have arms plus two longer tentacles.
visual: Side-by-side drawing: octopus vs squid

voiceover: Three hearts, blue blood, eight arms. Which ocean animal should I explain next?

voiceover: Fireflies make light without getting hot.
visual: Stock clip: fireflies glowing over a dark field

voiceover: Fireflies are beetles. Their glow comes from a chemical reaction in an organ at the tip of the belly.
visual: Simple diagram: firefly with glowing belly tip

voiceover: A chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by an enzyme called luciferase, and gives off light.
visual: Simple animation: two molecules meeting, then a glow

voiceover: Almost all of that energy becomes light, not heat. That is why it’s often called cold light.
visual: Simple graphic: light bulb versus firefly, heat icon

voiceover: The flashes are messages. In many species, males flash a pattern while flying, and females answer from the ground.
visual: Simple animation: flash in the air, reply below

voiceover: Each species has its own timing. The common eastern firefly makes a J-shaped flash as it swoops upward.
visual: Simple animation: J-shaped light trail

voiceover: Firefly larvae glow too, which may warn predators that they taste bad.
visual: Stock photo: glowing larva on soil

voiceover: A beetle that talks in light. When did you last see fireflies where you live?
visual: Wide shot of field with fireflies

voiceover: Penguins and polar bears never meet in the wild.
visual: Split-screen: penguin and polar bear, separate stock clips

voiceover: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Wild penguins live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.
visual: Map of range: Arctic versus Antarctica

voiceover: The emperor penguin, the largest penguin, breeds on the sea ice around Antarctica in winter.
visual: Stock clip: emperor penguins on ice

voiceover: The female lays one egg, then heads to sea to feed. The male balances the egg on his feet.
visual: Simple diagram: egg on feet under a skin flap

voiceover: He keeps it warm under a fold of skin for about two months, through storms and darkness, without eating.
visual: Stock clip: penguin shuffling with egg

voiceover: Thousands of males huddle together, slowly shuffling so each bird takes turns near the warm middle.
visual: Stock clip: large huddle from above

voiceover: When the chick hatches, the female returns with food, and the parents take turns feeding it.
visual: Stock clip: adult feeding a fluffy chick

voiceover: Wrong pole, right hero. Which polar animal should I cover next?
visual: Penguin colony, slow zoom out

voiceover: This mammal lays eggs and senses electricity.
visual: Stock clip: platypus swimming in a stream

voiceover: The platypus lives in rivers and streams in eastern Australia, including Tasmania.
visual: Map of range: eastern Australia and Tasmania

voiceover: It’s a mammal with fur and it feeds its young milk, but it lays eggs instead of giving birth.
visual: Simple checklist graphic: fur, milk, eggs

voiceover: It has no nipples. Milk seeps out through patches of skin, and the babies lap it up.
visual: Simple diagram: milk patches on the belly

voiceover: Underwater, it shuts its eyes, ears and nose. Its soft bill senses tiny electric signals from prey’s muscles.
visual: Simple animation: bill with electric ripples

voiceover: Males also have a spur on each back ankle that can deliver venom, painful but not deadly to people.
visual: Simple diagram: ankle spur highlighted

voiceover: Early European scientists who saw a preserved one first suspected it was a fake.
visual: Illustration: old drawing of a platypus

voiceover: One animal, many surprises. Which odd mammal should I cover next?

voiceover: This tiny frog gets its poison from its food.
visual: Stock clip: golden poison frog on a leaf

voiceover: The golden poison frog lives in a small patch of Colombian rainforest and is about 5 centimeters long.
visual: Map of range: western Colombia

voiceover: Its skin carries one of the strongest natural toxins known. Its bright yellow color warns predators away.
visual: Close-up stock clip of yellow skin

voiceover: Some Indigenous hunters in Colombia have used the toxin on the tips of blow-gun darts. That’s where the name comes from.
visual: Simple illustration: dart tip, no animals harmed

voiceover: But the frog doesn’t make the poison from scratch. Scientists think it builds it from small insects it eats in the wild.
visual: Simple graphic: ants and beetles into frog icon

voiceover: Frogs raised in zoos on other food lack the toxin. Their diet doesn’t contain the right ingredients.
visual: Stock clip: frog in a zoo terrarium

voiceover: So these are wild animals to watch, never to touch, wherever you meet them.
visual: Stock clip: frog on rainforest floor

voiceover: You are what you eat, literally. Which colorful animal should I cover next?
visual: Frog close-up, slow zoom

voiceover: Pigs aren’t dirty. They just can’t sweat much.
visual: Stock clip: pig lying in a mud wallow

voiceover: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they can’t cool down the way we do.
visual: Simple diagram: skin with few sweat glands

voiceover: On hot days, wet mud on the skin keeps cooling them as the water slowly evaporates.
visual: Simple animation: heat lines rising off mud

voiceover: A coat of mud also works as sunscreen and helps keep biting insects off their skin.
visual: Stock clip: pig shaking off mud

voiceover: Given room, pigs keep their sleeping area separate from their toilet area, often far apart.
visual: Simple graphic: pen with two zones

voiceover: They’re also smart. Pigs can learn to come when called and can solve simple puzzles.
visual: Stock clip: pig nudging an object with its snout

voiceover: Their wild relative, the wild boar, wallows too, so it’s an old habit, not a farm problem.
visual: Stock clip: wild boar in a forest

voiceover: Mud is a tool, not a mess. Which farm animal should I defend next?
visual: Pig close-up, slow zoom

voiceover: T. rex lived closer to you than to Stegosaurus.
visual: Illustration: T. rex and Stegosaurus silhouettes

voiceover: They often appear together in toys and cartoons. In real life, they never met.
visual: Simple graphic: toy box with two dinosaurs

voiceover: Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago.
visual: Timeline graphic: Stegosaurus at 150 million

voiceover: T. rex lived at the very end of the Cretaceous, about 68 to 66 million years ago.
visual: Timeline graphic: T. rex at 68 to 66 million

voiceover: That gap is over 80 million years. The gap between the last T. rex and you is about 66 million.
visual: Timeline graphic: two bars compared

voiceover: So T. rex is closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus. Dinosaurs were around for a very long time.
visual: Timeline graphic: zoom out across eras

voiceover: Both are known only from fossils. The dinosaurs that weren’t birds died out about 66 million years ago.

voiceover: Some living whales may be over 200 years old.
visual: Stock clip: bowhead whale surfacing among ice

voiceover: The bowhead whale lives its whole life in cold Arctic and sub-Arctic waters.
visual: Map of range: Arctic seas

voiceover: It has the thickest blubber of any whale, up to about half a meter, to stay warm in icy water.
visual: Simple diagram: blubber layer cross-section

voiceover: Its huge head can break through sea ice to make breathing holes.
visual: Stock clip: whale head breaking thin ice

voiceover: Clues to its age came from whales caught by Indigenous hunters in Alaska that carried old harpoon tips.
visual: Simple graphic: old harpoon tip, labeled 1800s

voiceover: Some of those tips were made in the 1800s. Scientists then estimated ages from chemistry in the whales’ eyes.
visual: Simple diagram: eye with an age clock

visual: Timeline graphic: 1800s to today

voiceover: In the dark deep sea, this fish carries light.
visual: Simple animation: one glowing dot in black water

visual: Simple diagram: ocean depth zones

voiceover: A spine on the female’s head works like a fishing rod, with a glowing lure on the tip.
visual: Simple drawing: anglerfish with rod and lure

voiceover: The glow comes from bacteria living inside the lure. Small animals swim toward the light.
visual: Simple animation: tiny fish drifting toward lure

voiceover: Food is scarce down there, so the anglerfish waits, and a large mouth lets it take what comes.
visual: Simple drawing: wide-mouthed fish waiting

visual: Simple drawing: tiny male attached to female

visual: Simple diagram: male joined to female

voiceover: These insects wait 17 years underground, then emerge together.
visual: Stock clip: cicada climbing a tree trunk

voiceover: Periodical cicadas live in the eastern United States. Young cicadas, called nymphs, live in the soil.
visual: Map of range: eastern United States

voiceover: They feed on fluid from tree roots for about 17 years, depending on the species and brood.
visual: Simple diagram: nymph beside a tree root

voiceover: Then, in spring, millions crawl out on the same few nights, climb trees and shed their skins.
visual: Stock clip: cicada shedding its skin

voiceover: One idea is safety in numbers. Predators can eat only so many, so plenty survive to breed.
visual: Simple graphic: predator icon full, many cicadas left

voiceover: Males sing loudly with drum-like organs on their bodies. Adults live only a few weeks.
visual: Simple diagram: sound organ on the body

voiceover: Early settlers called them locusts. They aren’t. Locusts are grasshoppers; cicadas are a different group.
visual: Split-screen: cicada and grasshopper drawings

voiceover: Seventeen years of waiting for a few weeks of song. Have you heard one?

voiceover: This bird doesn’t just use tools. It makes them.
visual: Stock clip: crow holding a stick in its beak

voiceover: The New Caledonian crow lives on islands in the South Pacific, east of Australia.
visual: Map of range: New Caledonia

voiceover: It pokes sticks into holes in dead wood to pull out beetle larvae hiding inside.
visual: Simple animation: stick reaching into a log

voiceover: Some crows snap twigs and carve a small hook at the end, which makes grabbing food easier.
visual: Simple drawing: twig with a hooked tip

visual: Simple drawing: stepped leaf tool

voiceover: Young crows learn by watching adults, and tool styles can differ from one area to another.
visual: Stock clip: young crow beside an adult

visual: Stock clip: crow with tool, close-up

voiceover: A bird with a toolbox. Which smart animal should I cover next?

voiceover: The biggest kangaroo starts life jellybean-sized.

voiceover: The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial, and adult males can stand taller than many people.
visual: Scale graphic: kangaroo next to a person outline

visual: Scale graphic: tiny newborn on a fingertip

voiceover: Right after birth, it crawls through its mother’s fur into her pouch, all on its own.

visual: Stock clip: kangaroo hopping across plain

voiceover: From jellybean to giant. Which marsupial should I cover next?

voiceover: This lizard can run across the top of water.
visual: Slow-motion stock clip: basilisk running on water

voiceover: The green basilisk lives in rainforests in Central America, often in trees near rivers.
visual: Map of range: Central America

voiceover: When startled, it drops to the water and sprints on its back legs, upright like a tiny runner.
visual: Stock clip: lizard dropping from a branch

voiceover: Its long back toes have flaps of skin that spread out and push against the surface.
visual: Simple diagram: toe flaps spread

visual: Simple animation: slap, air pocket, lift

voiceover: Smaller, lighter young lizards can run farther across water than heavy adults.
visual: Simple graphic: small lizard, long path; big lizard, short

visual: Stock clip: basilisk swimming

voiceover: Goats have rectangular pupils. There’s a reason.
visual: Close-up stock clip of a goat’s eye

voiceover: Many grazing animals, like goats, sheep and horses, have wide, horizontal pupils shaped like rectangles.
visual: Simple graphic: three eye shapes compared

voiceover: The wide shape gives them a broad, panoramic view along the ground, useful for spotting danger.
visual: Simple diagram: wide field of view around a goat

voiceover: When a goat lowers its head to graze, its eyes rotate so the pupils stay level with the horizon.
visual: Simple animation: head tilts, pupil stays level

voiceover: And goats don’t eat tin cans. They are picky browsers that prefer leaves, shrubs and twigs.
visual: Stock clip: goat nibbling a shrub

visual: Stock clip: goat mouthing a fence post

voiceover: Goats are also strong climbers, and some wild relatives scramble across steep, rocky cliffs with ease.
visual: Stock clip: wild goat on a rocky slope

voiceover: A sperm whale’s brain can weigh around 8 kilograms, about six times as much as a human brain.

voiceover: Dolphins sleep with half their brain awake.
