voiceover: Stars twinkle. Planets mostly shine steadily.
visual: Stock clip of a twinkling night sky

voiceover: The stars themselves aren't flickering. The twinkle happens in Earth's air, not in space.
visual: Simple diagram: star, atmosphere layer, eye

voiceover: Our atmosphere is full of moving pockets of warmer and cooler air that bend light slightly as it passes through.
visual: Animated icons: wavy air layers bending a light ray

voiceover: A star is so far away that it's basically a single point of light, so every tiny bend makes it jump and flicker.
visual: Simple graphic: single dot jittering

voiceover: Planets are much closer, so they appear as tiny disks. The flickers from different parts of the disk average out.
visual: Simple diagram: small disk made of many points

voiceover: That's a handy trick: if a bright dot shines steadily, there's a good chance it's a planet.
visual: Simple graphic: steady dot labelled planet

voiceover: Stars near the horizon twinkle most, because their light crosses more air. Astronauts above the air see steady stars.
visual: Simple diagram: long low light path vs short high path

voiceover: Have you used the twinkle test to find a planet? Tell me below.
visual: Star icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Neptune was predicted with math before it was spotted.
visual: Animated icons: equation lines turning into a blue planet

voiceover: In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't moving quite where its orbit said it should be.
visual: Simple diagram: predicted path vs actual path of Uranus

voiceover: Something unseen seemed to be tugging on it. A French mathematician, Urbain Le Verrier, worked out where that something must be.
visual: Animated icons: invisible tug arrow, pencil and paper

voiceover: In 1846, he sent his prediction to the Berlin Observatory, and astronomers there found the planet the very first night they looked.
visual: Simple sky chart with an X marking the spot

voiceover: It was within about one degree of the predicted spot, a tiny patch of sky.
visual: Simple graphic: small circle around the X

voiceover: An English mathematician, John Couch Adams, had made similar calculations, and both are now often credited.
visual: Simple graphic: two pencil icons side by side

voiceover: Neptune is so far out that one year there lasts about 165 Earth years. It finished its first full orbit since discovery in 2011.
visual: Animated diagram: one full orbit loop, 1846 to 2011

voiceover: Would you rather find a planet with math or a telescope? Comment below.
visual: Math and telescope icons + comment bubble

voiceover: Our Moon may have formed from a giant collision.
visual: Labelled artist's impression of two young worlds colliding

voiceover: The leading idea is that a Mars-sized body slammed into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
visual: Scale diagram: young Earth and a Mars-sized body

voiceover: Scientists often call that body Theia. The impact would have blasted molten rock and vapor into orbit around Earth.
visual: Animated icons: debris ring forming around Earth

voiceover: Over time, that debris clumped together and formed the Moon, possibly much closer to Earth than it is today.
visual: Animated diagram: ring clumping into a Moon

voiceover: Evidence: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo crews are strikingly similar to Earth's rocks in their chemistry.
visual: Simple graphic: two rock icons with matching labels

voiceover: The Moon also has a small iron core, which fits the idea that it formed mostly from rocky outer layers.
visual: Simple diagram: Moon cut-away with a small core

voiceover: Some details are still debated, like how much of the Moon came from Theia, but the collision idea leads the field.
visual: Simple graphic: question mark beside a leading badge

voiceover: Does a collision origin make the Moon more fascinating to you? Comment below.
visual: Moon icon + comment bubble

voiceover: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth.
visual: Stock clip of a green aurora

voiceover: Many people know the northern lights, but the southern lights are just as real, around the Antarctic region.
visual: Simple globe graphic: rings at both poles

voiceover: They start with the Sun, which constantly sends out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.
visual: Animated icons: particles streaming from the Sun

voiceover: Earth's magnetic field steers many of those particles toward the polar regions, where they slam into our upper atmosphere.
visual: Simple diagram: field lines guiding particles to the poles

voiceover: When they hit oxygen and nitrogen, those gases glow. Oxygen often gives green, and sometimes red at higher altitudes.
visual: Simple graphic: color key, green and red labelled oxygen

voiceover: Nitrogen can add blue and purple tints, which is why the edges of some displays look violet.
visual: Simple graphic: blue and purple swatches labelled nitrogen

voiceover: During big solar storms, auroras can reach much farther from the poles, and phone cameras often catch colors our eyes miss.
visual: Animated icons: phone camera showing brighter colors

voiceover: Northern or southern lights: which would you travel to see? Comment below.
visual: Aurora icons + comment bubble
